facts.statement: Mirischia was a coelurosaurian theropod dinosaur that lived in northeastern Brazil during the Early Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Mirischia is an extinct genus of coelurosaurian theropod dinosaur from the Albian stage (Early Cretaceous Period) of northeastern Brazil.

facts.statement: The species Mirischia asymmetrica was named and described in 2004 by David Martill, Eberhard Frey, and Darren Naish.
facts.quote: In 2004 the type species Mirischia asymmetrica was named and described by Martill, Frey and Darren Naish.

facts.statement: The specific name asymmetrica refers to the asymmetry between the left and right ischium in the fossil specimen.
facts.quote: The specific name asymmetrica refers to the fact that in the specimen the left ischium differs from its right counterpart.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen consists of a partial articulated skeleton including the pelvis, incomplete hind limbs, vertebrae, ribs, and thigh bones.
facts.quote: It consists of a partial articulated skeleton, largely consisting of the pelvis and incomplete hind limbs, including two posterior dorsal vertebrae, a rib, gastralia, partial ilia, pubes and ischia, partial thigh bones and the upper parts of the right tibia and fibula.

facts.statement: A piece of petrified intestine was preserved in front of the pubic bones of the holotype.
facts.quote: In front of the pubes, a piece of a petrified intestine is present.

facts.statement: Mirischia was a small bipedal predator.
facts.quote: Mirischia was a small bipedal predator.

facts.statement: In 2004, the length of Mirischia was estimated to be 2.1 meters.
facts.quote: Its length was in 2004 estimated at 2.1 metres (6.8 feet).

facts.statement: In 2010, Gregory S. Paul estimated the weight of Mirischia at seven kilograms.
facts.quote: In 2010 Gregory S. Paul estimated the weight at seven kilogrammes (15.4 pounds).

facts.statement: The ischia of Mirischia are asymmetrical, with the left bone having an oval hole and the right bone having an open notch.
facts.quote: The ischia of Mirischia are asymmetrical, that on the left being perforated by an oval foramen while that on the right has an open notch in the same position.

facts.statement: The specimen preserves soft tissue remains, including a vacuity interpreted as an air sac between the pubic and ischial bones.
facts.quote: The specimen is also unusual in that it preserves some soft tissue remains: apart from the intestine, what the describers interpreted to have been an air sac was preserved between its pubic and ischial bones in the form of a vacuity.

facts.statement: All skeletal elements of Mirischia exhibit an exceptionally thin bone wall.
facts.quote: Another notable trait is the exceptional thinness of the bone wall of all skeletal elements.

facts.statement: In 2004, Mirischia was classified within the Compsognathidae family.
facts.quote: In 2004 Mirischia was assigned to the Compsognathidae, as closely related to Compsognathus from the Upper Jurassic of Europe and Aristosuchus from the Lower Cretaceous of England.

facts.statement: In 2010, Darren Naish suggested that Mirischia might be a basal member of the Tyrannosauroidea.
facts.quote: In 2010 Naish suggested it may have instead been a basal member of the Tyrannosauroidea.

facts.statement: A 2024 study by Andrea Cau placed Mirischia in a polytomy within basal Coelurosauria, excluding it from the Compsognathus genus.
facts.quote: In 2024, Andrea Cau published a study on the phylogenetics of compsognathids that recovered Mirischia, along with four other proposed compsognathids in a polytomy within basal Coelurosauria.

facts.statement: Mirischia lived between 119.57 and 113.2 million years ago during the Aptian stage.
facts.quote: Time range: Aptian to Aptian (119.57 to 113.2 million years ago)
